Angela Merkel: Angela Dorothea Merkel (née Kasner; born 17 July 1954) is a German stateswoman and retired politician who served as Chancellor of Germany from 2005 to 2021.
In what year was Gerald Ford born?
Gerald Ford: Gerald Rudolph Ford Jr. (born Leslie Lynch King Jr.; July 14, 1913 – December 26, 2006) was the 38th president of the United States, serving from 1974 to 1977.
In what year did Madame du Barry die?
Madame du Barry: Jeanne Bécu, Comtesse du Barry (French: [baʁi]; 19 August 1743 – 8 December 1793) was the last maîtresse-en-titre of King Louis XV of France.

Cleopatra: Born in Alexandria, Cleopatra was the daughter of Ptolemy XII Auletes, who named her his heir before his death in 51 BC.

Rashidun Caliphate: The title Rashidun stems from the doctrine in Sunni Islam that the caliphs were "rightly guided".

Fall of Kabul (2021): Afghanistan. On 15 August 2021, Afghanistan's capital city of Kabul was captured by the Taliban after a major insurgent offensive that began in May 2021.
Pinkerton (detective agency): United States. It is currently a subsidiary of Swedish-based Securitas AB.

2004 Madrid train bombings: Spain. The explosions killed 193 people and injured around 2,500.

Battle of Chosin Reservoir: North Korea. The name "Chosin" is derived from the Japanese pronunciation "Chōshin", instead of the Korean pronunciation.

Swiss People's Party: Switzerland. Chaired by Marcel Dettling, it is the largest party in the Federal Assembly, with 62 members of the National Council and 6 of the Council of States.

History of Tibet: People's Republic of China. The Qing dynasty then sent military troops in the same year to fight the Dzungars, but failed.

Battle of the Frontiers: Belgium. The German concentration on the right (northern) flank, was to wheel through Belgium and attack the French in the rear.

Cultural Revolution: People's Republic of China. The Cultural Revolution, formally known as the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution, was a sociopolitical movement in the People's Republic of China (PRC).

Kingdom of Bavaria: German. The Kingdom of Bavaria was a German state that succeeded the former Electorate of Bavaria in 1806 and continued to exist until 1918.

Kingdom of Israel (Samaria): Hebrew. Its beginnings date back to the first half of the 10th century BCE.

Kingdom of Hungary (1920–1946): Hungarian. Republican Austria, the successor of the former other half of the dual monarchy also received some minor territory from Hungary.

Old Spanish is an official language of Crown of Castile. In 1492, the voyage of Christopher Columbus and the discovery of the Americas were major events in the history of Castile.

Described as 'the highest form of love, charity' and the mutual love between God and humanity, this Greek concept denotes a sacrificial love that persists regardless of circumstance, in contrast to brotherly or self-love — name this term?
Agape (from Ancient Greek (agp)) is "the highest form of love, charity" and "the love of God for and of for God".
Having first served as Iran's president in the 1980s, this Grand Ayatollah went on to a 36-year run as supreme leader — the longest of any head of state in West Asia of his era. Who was he?
Ali Khamenei (19 April 1939 - 28 February 2026) was an Iranian politician and Shia cleric who served as the second supreme leader of Iran from 1989 until his assassination in 2026.
Known as the 'Grand Marshal of Ayacucho,' this Venezuelan general and close ally of Simón Bolívar served as Bolivia's president from 1825 to 1828 — who is he?

Antonio José de Sucre (Spanish; 3 February 1795 - 4 June 1830), known as the "Gran Mariscal de Ayacucho", was a Venezuelan general and politician who served as the president of Bolivia from 1825 to 1828.
Elected four times to Karnataka's legislature from Shiggaon, this engineer-turned-politician later served as the state's 17th chief minister — who is he?

Basavaraj Bommai (born 28 January 1960) is an Indian politician and engineer who is currently serving as the Lok Sabha MP of Haveri and previously served as the 17th Chief Minister of Karnataka from 18 July 2021 to 19 May 2023.
A Rhodes Scholar at Oxford who led Australia's main trade-union council before entering politics, this Labor figure served as the country's 23rd prime minister from 1983 to 1991 — who was he?
Bob Hawke (9 December 1929 - 16 May 2019) was an Australian politician, trade unionist, economist and central banker who served as the 23rd prime minister of Australia from 1983 to 1991.
Paired with her daughter Proserpina in Roman religious rites, this agricultural goddess is the only farming deity among Rome's twelve major gods — who is she?
Ceres (mythology) was a goddess of agriculture, grain crops, fertility, and motherly relationships.

The first woman to serve as president of the Philippines, this politician led the 1986 People Power Revolution that ended Ferdinand Marcos's two-decade rule and has been dubbed the 'Mother of Democracy' — who was she?
Corazon Aquino (January 25, 1933 - August 1, 2009) was a Filipino politician who served as the 11th president of the Philippines, serving from 1986 to 1992.
Peru's first female president, she took office in December 2022 after serving as vice president, and was removed from power in October 2025 — who is she?
Dina Boluarte (born 31 May 1962) is a Peruvian politician, civil servant, and lawyer who served as the president of Peru from 7 December 2022 until she was removed from office on 10 October 2025.

This Mexican revolutionary and guerrilla leader championed the cause of peasant farmers in Morelos during the 1910–1920 Mexican Revolution, inspiring an entire agrarian movement named after him — who is he?
Emiliano Zapata (Latin American; 8 August 1879 - 10 April 1919) was a Mexican revolutionary and guerrilla leader.

Founded in 2009 by comedian Beppe Grillo, this Italian populist party rejected traditional left-right politics for years before recently identifying as 'independent progressives' — which party, now led by Giuseppe Conte?
Five Star Movement is a political party in Italy, led by Giuseppe Conte.
This Soviet politician briefly succeeded Joseph Stalin as Premier in 1953, before losing a power struggle with Nikita Khrushchev that cost him his post by 1955 — who is he?
Georgy Malenkov was Leader of the Soviet Union from 1953 to 1955.
A key figure in the 1963 coup that brought the Ba'ath Party to power, he ruled Syria as president from 1971 until his death in 2000 — and was succeeded by his son. Who was he?
Hafez al-Assad (6 October 1930 - 10 June 2000) was a Syrian politician and military officer who served as the president of Syria from 1971 until his death in 2000.

Ranging across traditions that can be polytheistic, monotheistic, monistic, or even agnostic, these divine figures are known by terms like Deva, Devi, Ishvara, and Bhagavan depending on the tradition — who are they?
Hindu deities are the gods and goddesses in Hinduism.

Along with the Thracians and Greeks, this Indo-European-speaking people made up one of the three main ancient populations of the Balkan Peninsula, inhabiting territory across modern Albania, Montenegro, and neighboring lands. Who were they?
Illyrians (Ancient) were a group of Indo-European-speaking people who inhabited the western Balkan Peninsula in ancient times.

A protégé of Andrew Jackson, this expansionist president saw Texas join the Union, pushed U.S. territory to the Pacific, and settled the Oregon dispute that drew today's U.S.-Canada line — who was he?
James K. Polk (November 2, 1795 - June 15, 1849) was the 11th president of the United States, serving from 1845 to 1849.
Nicknamed 'the Beautiful' and 'the Good,' this porphyrogennetos son of Alexios I ruled Byzantium from 1118 and set out to undo the damage of Manzikert — who was he?
Alfonso VI of León and Castile
John II Komnenos (13 September 1087 - 8 April 1143) was Byzantine emperor from 1118 to 1143.
The first woman elected to her union's negotiating team at a Kerr-McGee plutonium plant, she was found contaminated and died in a car crash en route to meet a New York Times reporter — who was she?

Karen Silkwood (February 19, 1946 - November 13, 1974) was an American laboratory technician and labor union activist known for reporting concerns about corporate practices related to health and safety in a nuclear facility.
This Arizona senator, who served from 2019 to 2025, left the Democratic Party to become an independent in December 2022 after previously serving in the state legislature — who is she?
Kyrsten Sinema (born July 12, 1976) is an American politician, lawyer, and former social worker who served from 2019 to 2025 as a United States senator from Arizona.
He supported Hitler's rearmament as army Chief of Staff but believed Germany wasn't ready for war, and ended up a ringleader of the 20 July assassination plot — who was this general?
Ludwig Beck (29 June 1880 - 20 July 1944) was a German general who served as Chief of the German General Staff from 1933 to 1938.

This queen consort of France and Navarre served as regent for her young son from 1610, refusing to relinquish power even after his legal coming-of-age in 1614, until a coup finally removed her in 1617. Who was she?
Marie de' Medici (26 April 1575 - 3 July 1642) was Queen of France and Navarre as the second wife of King Henry IV.

At Villers-Bocage in June 1944, this German Tiger-tank commander wrecked up to 14 tanks and 15 personnel carriers in a single 15-minute ambush, becoming a postwar 'panzer ace' cult figure — who was he?
Michael Wittmann (22 April 1914 - 8 August 1944) was a German Waffen-SS tank commander during the Second World War.
Notorious as much for his criminal reputation as his politics, this Uttar Pradesh figure held the Mau assembly seat across five election wins — who is he?
Mukhtar Ansari (30 June 1963 - 28 March 2024) was an Indian gangster and politician, based in Uttar Pradesh.
A journalist who once served a year in prison for defamation against a government minister, he later became the 16th prime minister of Armenia in 2018 — who is he?
Nikol Pashinyan (born 1 June 1975) is an Armenian politician who is serving as the 16th and current prime minister of Armenia since 2018.
Which Andean earth-and-time goddess, revered since Inca times, is said to have given birth to the sun god Inti and the moon goddess Mama Quilla?
Pachamama (Quechua) or Mama Pacha is the Andean deity representing space-time, revered by the peoples of the Andes.

Reigning nearly 32 years, the longest verified papacy after Saint Peter, this 19th-century pontiff convoked the First Vatican Council in 1868, which defined papal infallibility before adjourning for good in 1870 — who was he?

Pope Pius IX (born Giovanni Maria Battista Pietro Pellegrino Isidoro Mastai-Ferretti; 13 May 1792 - 7 February 1878) was head of the Catholic Church from 16 June 1846 until his death in February 1878.
Nicknamed 'electric brain' for his calm under pressure, this U.S. admiral commanded Task Force 16 at Midway, where American dive bombers sank four Japanese fleet carriers — who was he?
Raymond A. Spruance (July 3, 1886 - December 13, 1969) was a United States Navy admiral during World War II.
Fill in the blank: “____ (born March 7, 1963) is a Canadian serial rapist, murderer and disgraced former colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force.”

Russell Williams (criminal) (born March 7, 1963) is a Canadian serial rapist, murderer and disgraced former colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force. Williams was born in Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, England and his family later emigrated to Canada.
Fluent in Sinhala and Dhivehi from his early diplomatic postings in Sri Lanka, this Russian official has served as foreign minister since 2004, longer than anyone since the Soviet era — who is he?
Sergey Lavrov (born 21 March 1950) is a Russian diplomat who has served as Minister of Foreign Affairs since 2004.
This Italian businessman-turned-politician has run a football club since 2017 and took office as mayor of an Umbrian city in 2023 — who is he?
Stefano Bandecchi (born 4 April 1961) is an Italian politician and entrepreneur.

This Norwegian adventurer and ethnographer drifted 8,000 kilometers across the Pacific on a primitive hand-built raft in 1947, hoping to prove that ancient South Americans could have colonized Polynesia — who is he?
Thor Heyerdahl (Norwegian; 6 October 1914 - 18 April 2002) was a Norwegian adventurer and ethnographer with a background in biology with specialization in zoology, botany and geography.
A sub-orbital spaceflight participant as well as an undersea explorer, he co-founded a private equity firm and reached the poles and Seven Summits before conquering the ocean floor. Who is he?
Victor Vescovo (born February 10, 1966) is an American private equity investor, retired naval officer, sub-orbital spaceflight participant, and undersea explorer.
This Ohioan holds a singular distinction: he is the only person to have served as both U.S. president and chief justice of the United States. Who was he?
William Howard Taft (September 15, 1857 - March 8, 1930) was the 27th president of the United States from 1909 to 1913 and the tenth chief justice of the United States from 1921 to 1930.
A trained electrical engineer who dared to criticize Mao's economic policies in 1957 and got branded a 'rightist' for it, this man later served as China's premier from 1998 to 2003 — who is he?
Zhu Rongji (born 23 October 1928) is a Chinese retired politician and electrical engineer who served as the 5th premier of China from 1998 to 2003.
Allegedly the first Syrian to hold the position, this militant leader served as the fourth so-called caliph of the Islamic State from November 2022 until his death in April 2023. Who was he?
Abu al-Hussein al-Husseini al-Qurashi: Islamic State leader from 2022 to 2023.

Rising to lead the Goths after the Battle of Adrianople, this first king of the Visigoths — whose Gothic name meant 'ruler of all' — served under a Roman emperor before becoming Rome's fiercest adversary in the Balkans. Who was he?
Alaric I: King of the Visigoths from 395 to 410.
Formed in 1993 by merging a party from West Germany with one from East Germany, this party held 85 of the Bundestag's 630 seats after Germany's 2025 election — which party?
Alliance 90/The Greens: Green political party in Germany.
Born in Stockport and out of school at 16 without qualifications, this Labour MP later became the UK's Deputy Prime Minister before resigning in 2025 — who is she?
Angela Rayner: Deputy Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2024 to 2025.
Governing Japan from Kyoto during the Muromachi period, this feudal military government ran from 1336 to 1573 and began after overthrowing the Kenmu Restoration — which regime?

Ashikaga shogunate: Ruling military government of feudal Japan (1336–1573). The Ashikaga clan governed Japan from the Imperial capital of Heian-kyō (Kyoto) as de facto military rulers along with the daimyō lords of the samurai class.
An Arizona senator and Air Force Reserve major general who rejected the legacy of the New Deal, this conservative was the Republican Party's presidential nominee in 1964. Who is he?
Barry Goldwater: American politician and military officer (1909–1998)
Born in Montevideo during his father's exile, this Guatemalan sociologist-turned-politician co-founded the Semilla party and became his country's president in 2024 — who is he?
Bernardo Arévalo: President of Guatemala since 2024.
Per the Book of Genesis, God commanded Abraham toward this rite, traditionally performed by a mohel on a newborn boy's eighth day and followed by a celebratory meal — what is it?
End of World War II in Europe
Brit milah: Jewish religious male circumcision ceremony.

This ancient state, whose territory mostly overlapped modern Azerbaijan, gets its Western name from a Greek mistranslation of an Armenian term — which historical realm is this, whose descendants include the Udi people?

Caucasian Albania: Ancient state in the Caucasus. Caucasian Albania is a modern exonym for a former state located in ancient times in the Caucasus, mostly overlapping the region of present-day Azerbaijan.

The longest-serving leader of Germany's Free Democratic Party, this politician served as Federal Finance Minister until his 2024 dismissal, and his cabinet exit is seen as the catalyst for his party's 2025 parliamentary wipeout — who is he?
Elected to Newark's council after a 10-day hunger strike in a tent, this Rhodes Scholar became the city's 38th mayor before becoming New Jersey's first African-American U.S. senator — who is he?

The longest-serving prime minister of Iceland and former mayor of Reykjavík, he later chaired the Central Bank — and the 2008 financial crisis sparked loud public demands for his resignation. Who was he?

Born into a wealthy New York family and educated at the University of Pennsylvania, this real estate mogul became the 47th president after a career of branded towers, hotels, casinos, and side ventures — who is he?
Donald Trump: President of the United States (2017–2021; since 2025)
Succeeding Erich Honecker just weeks before the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, this politician became the last Communist leader of East Germany — who is he?
Egon Krenz: Leader of East Germany in 1989. Throughout his career, Krenz held a number of prominent positions in the SED.
A key figure of the Heroic Age of Antarctic Exploration, this Anglo-Irish explorer led three British expeditions south and set a new Farthest South record in 1909 — who was he?
A dependency-theory scholar before he was a head of state, this sociologist became the first Brazilian president to win re-election — who is he?
Fernando Henrique Cardoso: President of Brazil from 1995 to 2003.
Governing from 1946 to 1958, this parliamentary government presided over rapid postwar economic growth fueled by the Marshall Plan, despite chronic cabinet instability. What was it called?

French Fourth Republic: Government of France from 1946 to 1958. It also saw the beginning of the rapprochement with France's longtime enemy Germany, which led to Franco-German co-operation and eventually to the European Union.
This 43rd U.S. president served from 2001–2009. Born into a prominent political family, he was previously Texas governor and co-owned a baseball team. Who is he?
George W. Bush: President of the United States from 2001 to 2009.
In 2018, a 15-year-old skipped class to sit alone outside Sweden's parliament — and accidentally sparked the worldwide Fridays for Future movement. Which young climate activist was it?
Traditionally regarded as the first king to unify Norway into one kingdom, this 9th-century monarch was succeeded by his sons Eric Bloodaxe and Haakon the Good — who was he?
Harald Fairhair: Legendary first king of Norway. Harald Fairhair (Old Norse: Haraldr Hárfagri; c. 850 – c. 932) was a Norwegian king.
Also known as the White Huns, this Central Asian people defeated the Kidarites in 450 CE before falling to a joint Turkic-Sasanian force in 560 — who were they?
Hephthalites: 5th–8th-century nomadic confederation in Central Asia.
Adopted in 1917 to shed a German-sounding surname amid wartime sentiment, this royal lineage has included five monarchs, from George V to Charles III — which royal family?
House of Windsor: British royal family. The House of Windsor is the current royal house of the United Kingdom and other Commonwealth realms.
Known to the Akkadians as Ishtar and symbolized by a lion and an eight-pointed star, which Mesopotamian goddess of war and love was worshipped at a temple in Uruk?
Inanna: Ancient Mesopotamian goddess. Inanna was worshipped in Sumer as early as the Uruk period (c. 4000 – 3100 BCE), and her worship was relatively localized before the conquest of Sargon of Akkad.
A last-minute swap onto the Apollo 13 crew, this command module pilot rode the famous aborted mission farther from Earth than any astronaut would travel for decades — who was he?
Jack Swigert: American astronaut and politician (1931–1982)

Sister of a president, two U.S. senators, and the founder of the Special Olympics, this diplomat served as U.S. Ambassador to Ireland and convinced Bill Clinton to grant a controversial visa to a Sinn Féin leader — who is she?
Serving as regent of Hungary from 1446 to 1453, this military leader earned the nickname 'Turk-buster' for his campaigns against the Ottoman Empire — who is he?
John Hunyadi: Hungarian military and political figure (c. 1406–1456)

Having first crossed the Atlantic as a 'gentleman volunteer' on Columbus's second voyage, this conquistador later became the first governor of Puerto Rico and led the first European expedition to Florida in 1513. Who was he?
Juan Ponce de León: Spanish explorer and conquistador (1474–1521)
He left school at 12 to work the family farm yet rose to become both prime minister and, uniquely in his country's history, also governor-general of New Zealand — who was he?
The first UN Secretary-General to rise from within the organization's own staff, this Ghanaian diplomat shared the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize with the UN itself — who is he?
Kofi Annan: UN Secretary-General from 1997 to 2006.
This political ideology calls for a revolutionary vanguard party to lead a "dictatorship of the proletariat" as the prelude to communism — what is it named for its Russian architect?
Leninism: Political theory developed by Vladimir Lenin.
Nicknamed the "Citizen King," this last man to rule France with the title "King" came from the Orléans branch of the Bourbons and abdicated during the 1848 revolution — who was he?
Louis Philippe I: King of the French from 1830 to 1848.
Born in 1944, this Japanese politician is the daughter of a former prime minister and his official wife — who is she?
Elected to Congress in 2020 for Georgia's 14th district and known by her initials, this far-right politician has promoted QAnon and Pizzagate before resigning in 2026 — who is she?
Crowned sultan twice — once as a boy, once as a man who built up the Ottoman navy — he earned a nickname meaning 'the Father of Conquest' — which ruler?
Mehmed II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire (r. 1444–1446, 1451–1481)
This retired military officer studied law in Rangoon, led the Tatmadaw from 2011, and has ruled his country since seizing power in a February 2021 coup — who is he?
Min Aung Hlaing: Burmese politician and military officer (born 1956)
This young Arab commander, serving the Umayyad Caliphate, captured the region of Sindh around 712, marking the start of Muslim rule in South Asia — who is he?
Muhammad ibn al-Qasim: Umayyad general and governor of Sindh (695–715)

The principal wife of Ramesses the Great, this Egyptian queen was rare among her peers for being literate in hieroglyphs — a skill she used in royal diplomatic correspondence — and had her own temple built beside his at Abu Simbel. Who was she?
Nefertari: Wife of the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II.
A former steel worker who rose through the Soviet party ranks, he became the first president of Kazakhstan and ruled from 1991 to 2019 — who is he?

Nursultan Nazarbayev: President of Kazakhstan from 1991 to 2019. Nursultan Abishuly Nazarbayev (born 6 July 1940) is a Kazakh politician who served as the first president of Kazakhstan from 1991 to 2019.
Coined by French peace campaigner Émile Arnaud in 1901, this opposition to war and violence was embodied in Gandhi's philosophy of steadfast nonviolent resistance, 'satyagraha' — what is it?

Pacifism: Philosophy opposing war or violence. Its effectiveness served as inspiration to Martin Luther King Jr., James Lawson, James Bevel, Thích Nhất Hạnh, and many others in the civil rights movement.
Twice elected mayor of Washington D.C., this Whig newspaperman amassed one of the most extensive private collections of Revolutionary-era maps and manuscripts in America — who was he?
Peter Force: American politician and historian (1790–1868)

Marrying his first cousin, the reigning British queen, at age 20, this royal consort championed educational reform and the abolition of slavery, and organized the Great Exhibition of 1851 — who was he?
Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha: Consort of Queen Victoria from 1840 to 1861.
Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha
He became Britain's first Labour prime minister in 1924, then was expelled from his own party in 1931 for leading a Conservative-dominated National Government — who was he?
Ramsay MacDonald: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (1924; 1929–1935)
The first person to navigate the Northwest Passage by sea, this Norwegian explorer later led the first party to reach the South Pole aboard the ship Fram — who is he?
Beginning in October 1990, this conflict pitted the government's army against the Patriotic Front, a refugee-founded rebel force led in part by Paul Kagame, and ran until July 1994 — what was it?
Rwandan Civil War: 1990–1994 armed struggle in Rwanda.
Dominating the Pontic steppe from the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD, this confederation of ancient Iranian horse nomads formed part of the wider Scythian world — who were they?
Sarmatians: Large Iranian confederation that existed in classical antiquity.

Spurned in childhood as an illegitimate son, this early-19th-century monarch transformed his kingdom's army into a formidable fighting force during his reign from 1816 to 1828 — who was this Southern African king?
Shaka: Zulu king from 1816 to 1828. King Shaka was born in the lunar month of uNtulikazi (July) in 1787, in Mthonjaneni, KwaZulu-Natal Province, South Africa.
Stepping up from hostess for her assassinated husband, this Sri Lankan politician became, in 1960, the first woman in the world elected prime minister — who was she?
Sirimavo Bandaranaike: Prime Minister of Sri Lanka (1916–2000)
His was the longest reign of any Ottoman sultan, taking Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522 and shattering Hungary's army at Mohács in 1526 — who was this sultan?
Suleiman the Magnificent: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire (1520–1566)
Also called the Decalogue, these covenant directives were given to Moses atop Mount Sinai and later smashed after he found the Israelites worshipping a golden calf. What are they?
Ten Commandments: Biblical principles relating to ethics and worship.
Born in 1320, this ruler acceded to the throne in 1333 and became the last emperor of one dynasty and the first of its northern successor state after fleeing — who was he?
Toghon Temür: Emperor of Yuan dynasty from 1333 to 1368.
With Merlin's magic making him look like his rival Gorlois, this legendary British king slept with Lady Igraine and fathered a certain 'once and future king' — who was he?
Uther Pendragon: Father of King Arthur in Arthurian legend.
Credited with coining the phrase 'sovereign democracy' while shaping Kremlin strategy for over a decade, this close Putin aide earned the nickname 'grey cardinal' — who is he?

A vaudeville-trained humorist born a citizen of the Cherokee Nation and known as 'Oklahoma's Favorite Son,' he made 71 films and wrote over 4,000 newspaper columns before dying in a 1935 plane crash — who was he?
Will Rogers: American humorist and entertainer (1879–1935)
This Pakistani general became the country's third president under martial law in 1969, and his tenure oversaw the war that led to Bangladesh's independence — who was he?
Yahya Khan: President of Pakistan from 1969 to 1971.
This ancient Iranian faith centers on the Avesta and reveres Ahura Mazda as the supreme, uncreated deity, teaching a struggle between Asha (truth) and Druj (the lie). What religion is it?
Zoroastrianism: Iranian religion founded by Zoroaster.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Patrick Geddes (born 1854) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Stephen Hales (born 1677) is the earliest of the four.
Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
C (programming language) (founded 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Pope Sylvester II is an astronomer.
Which one below is best known as a mathematician?
Eric Weinstein is a mathematician. Eric Ross Weinstein (born October 26, 1965) is an American investor and podcast host.
What is the atomic number of Radium?
Radium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ra and atomic number 88.
What is the atomic number of Zinc?
Zinc is a chemical element; it has symbol Zn and atomic number 30.
In what year did Stephen Hawking die?
Stephen Hawking: Hawking was born in Oxford into a family of physicians.
In what year was Theobroma cacao discovered?
Theobroma cacao (cacao tree or cocoa tree) is a small (6–12 m (20–39 ft) tall) evergreen tree in the Malvaceae family.
Mikoyan MiG-31: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The MiG-31 is the fastest known operational combat aircraft, with a top speed around 3,000 km/h (1,600 knots).
Which company manufactures CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder?
CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group. The JF-17 can be used for multiple roles, including interception, ground attack, anti-ship, and aerial reconnaissance.
In which country did the CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder take place?
CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: People's Republic of China. The JF-17 can be used for multiple roles, including interception, ground attack, anti-ship, and aerial reconnaissance.
Who is credited with discovering Darmstadtium?
GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research
Darmstadtium: GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research. Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Ds and atomic number 110.
Who is credited with discovering 2 Pallas?
2 Pallas: Heinrich Wilhelm Olbers. Pallas (minor-planet designation: 2 Pallas) is the third-largest asteroid in the Solar System by volume and mass.
Who is credited with discovering Multiple sclerosis?
Multiple sclerosis: Jean-Martin Charcot. It is a type of demyelinating disease, where the nervous system's ability to transmit signals is damaged.
People with this anxiety disorder dread places they feel they can't escape — crowds, queues, public transit — and in severe cases may become unable to leave home at all. What is it?
Agoraphobia is an anxiety disorder characterized by symptoms of anxiety in situations where the person perceives their environment to be unsafe with no way to escape.
Found on every continent but Antarctica and almost always monogamous breeders, which bird family unites ducks, geese, and swans under one scientific name?
Anatidae are the biological family of water birds that includes ducks, geese, and swans.
Considered a visual art even though it leans on civil engineering, this discipline gives us cultural symbols that often outlast the civilizations that built them. What is it?
Architecture is the study and practice of designing structures, especially habitable ones.
Native to the Mekong and Chao Phraya river basins, this freshwater catfish is marketed in the US as "swai" and in the UK as "river cobbler" — which fish?

Basa (fish) (Pangasius bocourti), as it is commonly referred to, is a species of primarily freshwater-dwelling catfish in the shark-catfish family, Pangasiidae, native to the Mekong and Chao Phraya river basins of Mainland Southeast Asia.
A flowering vine native to South Asia, this plant's small dried red drupes become the world's most traded spice, its final coloring depending on how ripe the fruit was when harvested — which spice?
Black pepper (Piper nigrum) is a flowering vine in the family Piperaceae, cultivated for its fruit (the peppercorn), which is usually dried and used as a spice and seasoning.
Also known as undulant fever and Malta fever, this zoonotic illness spreads mainly through drinking unpasteurized milk and is caused by tiny coccobacilli — what is it?
Brucellosis is a zoonosis (zoonotic disease) spread primarily via ingestion of unpasteurized milk from infected animals.
This medical specialty diagnoses and treats congenital heart defects, valvular disease, and heart failure, and is a sub-specialty of internal medicine — which field?
Cardiology (from Ancient Greek (kardi) 'heart' and - (-logia) 'study') is the study of the heart.

Doctors monitor blood levels every two days when giving this last-resort antibiotic, since its side effects include bone marrow suppression and, in infants, a swollen-stomach condition known as gray baby syndrome — what drug is it?
Chloramphenicol is an antibiotic useful for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.

Produced by a mammal's mammary glands in the first days after birth, this antibody-rich milk helps protect newborns like calves and human infants from infection before regular milk takes over — which substance?
Colostrum (from Latin, of unknown origin), also known as foremilk, is the milk expressed by the mammary glands of a female mammal during the first few days following delivery of the newborn.
Usually viral and often worse at night, this childhood respiratory infection swells the windpipe to produce a barking, brassy cough and noisy breathing — what's the condition?
Its genus name translates to 'two-crested lizard,' honoring the twin head-crests found on fossils unearthed in Arizona in the 1940s — which Early Jurassic predator is this?
Dilophosaurus (dy-, -foh-) is a genus of theropod dinosaurs that lived in what is now North America during the Early Jurassic, about 186 million years ago.

Specializing in legislative process and authoritarian rule, this Russian scholar became a fellow at a Berlin academy and hosts her own political radio talk show, reaching a million YouTube subscribers by 2022 — who is she?
Ekaterina Schulmann (ne Zaslavskaya; born 19 August 1978) is a Russian political scientist specializing in legislative processes and authoritarian governance.
This flammable, colorless solvent smells sweetly of pear drops and shows up in glues and nail polish remover — and it's also the ester used to gently strip caffeine from tea and coffee. What is it?
Ethyl acetate (commonly abbreviated EtOAc or EA) is the organic compound with the formula CH3CO2CH2CH3, simplified to C4H8O2.

Also known as Lasègue–Falret syndrome after the pair of psychiatrists who first described it, this shared delusional disorder is named for the small number of people who typically experience it together — what is it called?

Folie à deux (French for 'madness of two'), also called shared psychosis or shared delusional disorder (SDD), is a rare psychiatric syndrome in which symptoms of a delusional belief are "transmitted" from one individual to another.
Ordained a priest in 1923, this Belgian physicist connected an expanding universe to Einstein's field equations and floated an early Big Bang hypothesis — who was he?
Georges Lemaître (lə-MET-rə; 17 July 1894 - 20 June 1966) was a Belgian Catholic priest, theoretical physicist, and mathematician who made major contributions to cosmology and astrophysics.
A French polymath dabbling in anthropology, medicine and physics, he's best remembered for an 1895 book that became a seminal work of crowd psychology — who was he?
Gustave Le Bon (7 May 1841 - 13 December 1931) was a leading French polymath whose areas of interest included anthropology, psychology, sociology, medicine, invention, and physics.
Serving as both Reichsbank president and Minister of Economics under Hitler, this economist was credited with Germany's 1930s 'economic miracle' even as he opposed aspects of rearmament — who is he?
Hjalmar Schacht (22 January 1877 - 3 June 1970) was a German economist, banker, politician, and co-founder of the German Democratic Party.

This nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treats pain, fever, and inflammation — from migraines to arthritis — and typically starts working within an hour, whether taken orally or intravenously. What drug?
Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that is used to relieve pain, fever, and inflammation.
This Brussels chemist ran a famous five-year willow tree experiment and coined the word 'gas' from the Greek for chaos — who was he?
Jan Baptist van Helmont (12 January 1580 - 30 December 1644) was a chemist, physiologist, and physician from Brussels.
Linked to a herpesvirus and immune suppression, this cancer causing purple skin lesions was already being described by Hippocrates in the 300s BC — which condition?
Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a type of cancer that can form masses on the skin, in lymph nodes, in the mouth, or in other organs.

Which citrus-scented perennial herb in the mint family, whose genus name Melissa comes from the Greek for 'honey bee,' is naturalized worldwide after originating in the Mediterranean and Central Asia?
Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the mint family.
Dubbed the 'Queen of QVC' for her long-running shopping show and holding over 120 patents, this American entrepreneur is also an investor on the reality series Shark Tank — who is she?
Lori Greiner is an American television personality and entrepreneur.

This Milanese thinker was the first woman to write a mathematics handbook and the first appointed a mathematics professor — though she spent her final decades on theology and serving the poor. Who was she?
Maria Gaetana Agnesi (16 May 1718 - 9 January 1799) was a Milanese mathematician, philosopher, theologian, and humanitarian.

This American theoretical physicist and science communicator, a professor at the City College of New York, won a 2021 lifetime achievement award named for a famous science-fiction author, honoring his work bridging science and sci-fi. Who is he?
Michio Kaku (born January 24, 1947) is an American theoretical physicist, science communicator, futurologist, and writer of popular science.
One of the four basic animal tissue types, this contractile tissue comes in skeletal, cardiac, and smooth forms and relies on the proteins actin and myosin to generate movement — name the tissue?
Muscle is a specialised soft tissue, one of the four basic types of animal tissues.
This nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug treats acute pain and osteoarthritis by blocking prostaglandin production, though it carries a risk of liver side effects. Name the drug?
Nimesulide is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with pain medication and fever reducing properties.
Found on every continent except Antarctica, this fish-eating raptor nests near water and can be identified by its brown back and pale, grayish head — what bird is it?
Osprey (Pandion haliaetus), historically known as sea hawk, river hawk, and fish hawk, is a diurnal, fish-eating bird of prey with a cosmopolitan range.
Innervated by two dedicated nerves and inserting near the upper arm's bicipital groove, which broad chest muscle flexes and internally rotates the humerus?
Pectoralis major (from Latin pectus 'breast') is a thick, fan-shaped or triangular convergent muscle of the human chest.
This French physicist shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife, making them the first married couple ever to win a Nobel — who is he?
Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 - 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
Domesticated roughly 8,000 years ago in Southeast Asia, chickens are the most common example of this category of farmed birds — what's the term?
Poultry are domesticated birds kept by humans for the purpose of harvesting animal products such as meat, eggs or feathers.

The sole species in its genus within the same plant family as apples and pears, this deciduous tree produces a hard, aromatic golden-yellow fruit that's tart raw but turns into jam when cooked — name the fruit?
Quince (Cydonia oblonga) is the sole member of the genus Cydonia in the Malinae subtribe (which contains apples, pears, and other fruits) of the Rosaceae family.
First created near Darmstadt in 1994 and named for the physicist who discovered X-rays, this extremely radioactive element exists as only a handful of atoms with no practical use — which one is it?
Roentgenium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Rg and atomic number 111.
Found on every continent but Antarctica and numbering over 2,500 species, this eight-legged arachnid curves a stinger-tipped tail over its back — what is it?

Scorpion (order Scorpiones) are predatory arachnids with eight legs, a pair of grasping pincers (or Chelae) and a narrow, segmented tail, often carried in a characteristic forward curve over the back and always ending with a stinger.
Typically a bony enclosure around a vertebrate's brain, though cartilage in some fish and amphibians, this head structure combines a neurocranium with a facial skeleton — name it?

Skull is typically a bony enclosure around the brain of a vertebrate. In a human, the skull comprises two prominent parts: the neurocranium and the facial skeleton, which evolved from the first pharyngeal arch.
Named from the Greek word for tallow, this soft waxy 18-carbon saturated fatty compound is common in animal fats like beef tallow and lard — what is it called?
Stearic acid (stee-) is a saturated fatty acid with an 18-carbon chain.
A staple corm across African, Caribbean, Oceanian, and Asian cultures, this root vegetable of the arum family is often likened to yams — what is it?
Taro (Colocasia esculenta) is a root vegetable.

Affecting roughly 10 to 15 percent of people, this condition causes a person to hear ringing or other sounds with no external source, and its name comes from the Latin word for 'to ring' — what is it?
Tinnitus is a condition when a person hears a ringing sound or a different variety of sounds when no corresponding external sound is present and that other people cannot hear.
This bodily fluid, produced by the kidneys to flush out urea and other waste, can also serve a second life as a nitrogen-rich fertilizer for soil — what is it?
Urine is the fluid excreted by the kidneys of vertebrates to clear the bloodstream of excess water and metabolic by-products including urea, uric acid, and creatinine.
Packing a mass comparable to the Sun into a volume the size of Earth, this dense stellar remnant radiates residual heat rather than nuclear fusion — what is it?
White dwarf is a very dense type of star: in an Earth-sized volume, it packs a mass that is comparable to the Sun.
The only living member of its entire mammalian order, this nocturnal African burrower uses its long snout and powerful claws to dig ants and termites out of their mounds — what animal is it?
Aardvark: Burrowing mammal native to Africa.
While bacteria and some plants may be biologically immortal, this universal process in humans slows reaction time even as knowledge tends to grow — what is it called?
Ageing: Biological process of getting older.
Though commonly called a nut, this tree's fruit is technically a drupe with a hard shell surrounding an edible seed, closely related to the peach — which food is it?
Almond: Species of nut. The fruit of the almond is a drupe, consisting of an outer hull and a hard shell with the seed, which is not a true nut.
This Manchester physicist shared the 2010 Nobel Prize for his work on graphene — and is the only person to also hold an Ig Nobel, won for levitating a frog with magnetism. Who is he?
In this severe blood disorder, the bone marrow stops producing red cells, white cells and platelets alike, and about half of all cases have no known cause — what condition is it?
Aplastic anemia: Disease causing insufficient blood cells of all types.
From the Greek for 'lack of order,' this neurological sign involves loss of voluntary muscle coordination, often linked to cerebellum dysfunction — what is it called?
Ataxia: Neurological impairment of voluntary muscle movement.
A tender herb of the mint family native from Central Africa to Southeast Asia, its Genovese or 'sweet' variety is a kitchen staple worldwide — what is it?
Basil: Culinary herb. Basil (Ocimum basilicum), also called great basil, is a culinary herb of the family Lamiaceae (mints).

Named after two French physicists who discovered it in 1820, this equation in magnetostatics relates a magnetic field to the strength, direction, and distance of an electric current — which physics rule?
Biot–Savart law: Law of classical electromagnetism.
This rigid organ not only supports the body and enables movement but also manufactures both red and white blood cells and stores essential minerals — what is it?
Bone: Rigid organs of the skeleton of vertebrates.

Marketed as Wellbutrin, this atypical antidepressant doubles as a stop-smoking aid and stands out for not causing sexual dysfunction or weight gain — what is this norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor?
Bupropion: Medication mainly used for depression and smoking cessation.
Also known as Flinders rose, this perennial shrub with rounded fleshy leaves and white-to-pink flowers is native across circum-Mediterranean countries — what's the plant called?
Marketed as a COX-2 inhibitor, this NSAID treats arthritis pain and menstrual cramps but carries heart attack and stroke risk warnings — which drug?

This antibiotic is used as an eye ointment for conjunctivitis and, when safer options fail, to treat meningitis, plague, cholera, and typhoid — but in newborns it can trigger a dangerous swelling condition called gray baby syndrome — what drug is it?
Chloramphenicol: Antibiotic. Chloramphenicol is an antibiotic useful for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
Striking at the same hour every day for weeks at a time, usually around one eye, this excruciating neurological condition is considered one of the most painful known to medicine — what is it?
Cluster headache: Neurological disorder. The disease is considered among the most painful conditions known to medical science.

Native to Europe and North Africa, this member of the carrot family can grow to 8 feet tall, with hollow stems blotched dark maroon and a distinctly foul smell carried on the wind — which highly poisonous plant is this?
Conium maculatum: Poisonous plant. The plant is herbaceous, with no woody parts, and has a biennial lifecycle.
Commonly called comb jellies, these are the largest animals that swim using rows of cilia, drifting through every ocean as masses of two-layered jelly — what's the phylum?
Ctenophora: Phylum of gelatinous marine animals.
From muntjac to moose, members of the family Cervidae shed and regrow bony skull extensions each year — antlers used to battle rivals. What hoofed ruminant is this?
Deer: Family of hoofed mammals. A deer (pl.: deer) or true deer is a hoofed ruminant ungulate of the family Cervidae (informally the deer family).
Bred around 1890 by a Thuringian tax collector looking for a loyal guard dog, this sleek, high-alert German breed traditionally had its ears cropped and tail docked — which breed?
Dobermann: Black and tan dog breed from Germany.
Having studied mathematics under Karl Weierstrass, which philosopher founded the school of phenomenology and argued that transcendental consciousness sets the limits of all possible knowledge?
Coiled to just 6 to 7 centimetres but stretching nearly 20 feet if unraveled, this tube connects each testicle to the vas deferens and stores maturing sperm — what is it?

Epididymis: Tube that connects a testicle to a vas deferens. The epididymis serves as an interconnection between the multiple efferent ducts at the rear of a testicle (proximally), and the vas deferens (distally).
The most widely distributed member of its subfamily, this semiaquatic, fish-eating mustelid ranges across Europe, much of Asia, and North Africa's Maghreb — which animal?
Likely domesticated from the European polecat, with which it can still interbreed to produce hybrids, this slender mustelid averages about 50 centimeters long — what is it?
This Italian-American economist taught at MIT's Sloan School and Carnegie Mellon before collecting the 1985 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics. Who was he?
Franco Modigliani: Italian-American economist and Nobel Laureate (1918–2003)

Sold under a non-proprietary name once the original patent expires, this type of medication shares the same active ingredient as its brand-name predecessor, though packaging and coloring may differ — what's it called?
Generic drug: Pharmaceutical equivalent to a brand-name product.
First selectively bred for color in imperial China over 1,000 years ago, which popular aquarium pet has become an invasive pest after being released into rivers in North America and Australia?
Goldfish: Freshwater fish common in aquariums.
Making its first flight in 2001 and entering Indian Air Force service in 2015, this delta-wing multirole fighter is the smallest and lightest supersonic jet of its generation — which aircraft?
HAL Tejas: Indian combat aircraft. The aircraft made its first flight in 2001 and entered into service with the IAF in 2015.
This Michigan farm boy left home at 16 for Detroit, later patented the Model T's transmission, and gave his name to a whole system of mass production. Who was he?
This British Egyptologist discovered the untouched tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings in November 1922 — who is he?
Howard Carter: British archaeologist and Egyptologist (1874–1939)
This family of long-legged wading birds that live in wetlands and forests lent its name — mistakenly — to the scientific name of the western cattle egret in 1757 — what's the bird group called?
Ibis: Long-legged wading birds with down-curved beaks.
Sold under the brand name Accutane, this vitamin A-related retinoid treats severe cystic acne but commonly causes dry lips, dry skin, and increased sunburn risk — what is it called?
Isotretinoin: Medication primarily used to treat severe acne.
This German craftsman's mechanical printing press — with its oil-based ink and adjustable metal type — sparked an information revolution that helped fuel the Renaissance and Reformation — who is he?
Johannes Gutenberg: German inventor and craftsman (c. 1393–1406 – 1468)
This Canadian atmospheric scientist holds a chair in public policy at Texas Tech and in 2021 became chief scientist of the Nature Conservancy — who is she?
Katharine Hayhoe: Canadian atmospheric scientist. Katharine Anne Scott Hayhoe (born 1972) is a Canadian atmospheric scientist.
This broadly distributed genus of spiders is informally known as the widow spiders, including the black widow and brown widow — what is it called?
Latrodectus: Genus of spiders. Latrodectus is a broadly distributed genus of spiders informally called the widow spiders, with several species that are commonly known as the true widows.
Creator of both a widely used open-source operating system kernel and the version-control system Git, this engineer won the 2012 Millennium Technology Prize — who is he?
Linus Torvalds: Finnish and American software engineer (born 1969)
Described in the New Testament as a physician, this traditional author of two New Testament books is said to have been martyred by hanging from an olive tree — who is he?
Luke the Evangelist: One of the four traditionally ascribed authors of the canonical gospels.
Also known as sapodilla, this evergreen tree native to Mexico and Central America was carried to the Philippines by Spanish colonizers — which species?
Manilkara zapota: Species of tropical evergreen tree.
Native to Indomalaya and Australasia, this deciduous member of the mahogany family goes by names like chinaberry tree and Persian lilac — what is it?
A self-taught Soviet tinkerer who later became a lieutenant general, he designed a famously reliable assault rifle but felt sorrow at how widely it spread — who was he?
With roughly 200 species across 16 genera, this family of elongated fish is almost exclusively marine, with a name traced back through Portuguese and Latin to a Greek word — which family?
Moray eel: Family of fishes. Moray eels, or Muraenidae, are a family of eels whose members are found worldwide.
Sold under the brand name Revia, this medication blocks opioid receptors to reduce cravings in alcohol and opioid use disorders and is combined with bupropion to treat obesity — what is it?
Naltrexone: Medication. It has also been found to be effective for the treatment of other addictions and may be used for them off-label.
Humphry Davy coined this colorless gas's cheerful nickname for the euphoria it brings, and it still earns a spot on the WHO's Essential Medicines list for dentistry and surgery. What is it?
Nitrous oxide: Colourless non-flammable greenhouse gas.

A subdiscipline of metaphysics, this philosophical study of being asks what reality's most general features are, sorting things into particulars like Socrates and universals like the color green — what is it?
Ontology: Philosophical study of being. For example, social ontology examines basic concepts used in the social sciences.
This cat-family genus contains the five biggest living cats — jaguar, leopard, lion, snow leopard, and tiger — plus extinct relatives like the cave lion and American lion. Which genus is it?
Developed at Abbott Laboratories in 1930 and nicknamed 'yellow jackets' for its brand-name capsule color, this barbiturate is used in veterinary euthanasia and some U.S. executions — what drug is it?
Enclosed in a papery husk derived from its calyx, this nightshade genus includes the tomatillo and Cape gooseberry among its edible-fruited species — which genus?
Most commonly referring to a type called PET, this category of polymers built from ester linkages is often blended with cotton to reduce wrinkling — what is it called?
Polyester: Category of polymers, in which the monomers are joined together by ester links.
This deciduous member of the rose family includes many varieties known as plums in English, with greengages and damsons among its subspecies — which species is it?
Prunus domestica: Species of flowering plant.

Historically nicknamed 'hydrophobia' because sufferers panic at the offer of a drink, this viral disease causes severe brain inflammation and is virtually always fatal once symptoms appear. What is it?
Rabies: Deadly viral disease, transmitted through animals.
Nicknamed golden root or Arctic root, this Crassulaceae plant is popular in herbal supplements even though the FDA has warned sellers against overselling its health benefits — which plant?
Rhodiola rosea: Species of flowering plant in the stonecrop family.
A synthetic element named for a famous physicist, it's the first of the super-heavy transactinides and behaves chemically as the heavier cousin of hafnium in group 4 — which element?
Rutherfordium: Chemical element with atomic number 104 (Rf)
Nicknamed 'Devil's Breath' and derived from nightshade plants, which motion-sickness drug has also been used historically as a deliriant?
Made up of the collarbone, the scapula, and the upper-arm bone meeting in a ball-and-socket joint, which body part lets the arm swing in a full circle?
Shoulder: Part of the body. The articulations between the bones of the shoulder make up the shoulder joints.
Mostly made from potato starch but also found in apples and berries, this slowly-metabolized sugar alcohol is an isomer of mannitol, differing only at one hydroxyl group. What is it?

In probability theory, this mathematical concept models a family of random variables indexed often by time, used to describe things like bacterial growth or a gas molecule's erratic path — what is it called?
Stochastic process: Collection of random variables. Stochastic processes are widely used as mathematical models of systems and phenomena that appear to vary in a random manner.
This medical term describes a resting heart rate that exceeds 100 beats per minute — what is it?
Tachycardia: Heart rate exceeding normal resting rate.
The principal bitter alkaloid of the cacao plant, this caffeine cousin is found in chocolate, tea, and the kola nut, and works by blocking adenosine receptors. What is it?
Theobromine: Bitter alkaloid of the cacao plant. Theobromine, also known as xantheose, is the principal alkaloid of Theobroma cacao (cacao plant).

Though most often viral, this throat condition turns into the dreaded 'strep throat' when group A streptococcus is to blame, and can leave you with a sore throat, fever, and swollen glands — what is it?
Developed by Microsoft, this open-source language layers optional static typing onto JavaScript and transpiles back into it for use on both browsers and servers — what is it?
TypeScript: Programming language and superset of JavaScript.

Prized by the Inca, who reserved its ultra-fine wool for royalty alone, this wild Andean camelid is now believed to be the ancestor of the domesticated alpaca and is Peru's national animal — what is it?
Native to the high Himalayas, this large, shaggy bovine, scientific name Bos mutus, is the ancestor of the domesticated Bos grunniens — which animal?

While still a teenager, this French mathematician solved a 350-year-old problem about which polynomials can be solved by radicals, laying the groundwork for group theory, before dying from wounds suffered in a duel — who was he?
The symbol for neodymium is Nd. Neodymium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nd and atomic number 60.

Patek Philippe: Swiss luxury watch and clock manufacturer.
